segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Do you think eventually AI will become so powerful that it's inevitable the public will arrive at an answer, despite the government obfuscation and unwillingness to be open? I'm constantly blown away, Jacques, by the growing intelligence of AI and its capabilities. Is it possible that AI will give us an answer before the president does?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I'm very skeptical, and I'm here in Silicon Valley networking with people who are developing and funding AI. As you know, I've invested in a number of AI companies, including in medicine, including in surgery, with robots that were intelligent enough to work by themselves and operate with radiation inside the body. And those companies we've taken public. So AI can do a lot of things. AI has existed for the last 20 years, it's been in hospitals, in factories and so on, and it's wonderful and it's a great help in pushing science. Yes, AI already does that in astrophysics for example, and certainly in biology. But the data has been filtered. The data has been filtered by humans, by people in hospitals, by people in observatories who had precise definitions for what they were looking at. Now, they may not understand the total phenomenon, and AI is an extraordinary tool for a scientist to understand the phenomenon he's looking at. But this is not the AI you want.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Let me give you the only analogy I can think of: the Vietnam War. The Pentagon, and some of the people who have our data now, would remember that because they were involved in the Vietnam War. There were statistics on the computer every day. They were getting massive amounts of data from the field, from combat units, they were putting that on the computer. And then a couple of analysts in the Pentagon started thinking: why don't we go to Vietnam and talk to the guys there, to find out how the database corresponds to what's going on in the real fighting? And they would go there, they would find a bunch of people in a unit somewhere, and they would say: we've got this thing here from the database that said you're controlling this territory, things are pretty good. And the guys would laugh and they would say: well, we go every night to the places where the VC isn't, because we're completely outnumbered here, and if we go to the left we're going to be killed because we don't have the reinforcements we need. And so, why didn't you send that to the Pentagon? Well, they don't want to hear that.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I think we have the same situation here. You have a bunch of data, and they are acquiring more and more data to put on top of it. So sure, you can have a million cases in a big computer, with very good people analyzing it, doing statistics. They've never talked to this witness in the field whom I've met, and I've met his family. I've been there, and I say: there's going to be disclosure that this is real. And they'll say: Jacques, you're crazy, you've been here three times, we've shown you the traces, we told you the dog went back into the house. The guard dog went back into the house — that's a job, the guard dog wanted nothing to do with it, controlling the cows or the bulls. It wanted nothing to do with what was there.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And to continue your Vietnam analogy there, Jacques, of course the truth about Vietnam was only subsequently released by Daniel Ellsberg in the Pentagon Papers, where he revealed in a massive leak to the New York Times and the Washington Post the dirty secrets of the Vietnam War. It kind of begs the question: are we ever really going to know the full truth about disclosure without a massive leak? Is there going to have to be a catastrophic disclosure before we all get told what the government really knows, if the government knows anything at all?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Well, this is a social phenomenon, not just a scientific question, and I'm not a sociologist, as you know. There are a number of people entering the field now who are looking at the psychology, the sociology of the phenomenon, and I think those will have the answer. I see my role now — I'm changing my role again — I want to be a resource person. I'm not a whistleblower. People have the impression, and you probably do as well, that things are moving towards disclosure. They are. But the need is moving the other way: it's going darker, deeper and deeper. The group that has the database now is going around the world, because I have correspondents everywhere, and they say: oh, we've had three officers from the Pentagon here and it's great, they wanted our data and they asked all the right questions. So that investigation is going on. It is going on today, in the open, around the world. In the meantime, the data itself, whoever is in charge of it will have to reconstruct all this with a new team on the ground.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Absolutely. So Jacques, your book Forbidden Science 7 covers the period 2020 to 2025. What did you learn by 2025 that you didn't know in 2020? What was the big revelation in that half-decade period?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I think the biggest conclusion is that we have been working at the wrong level. We've been doing what people always do: they assume they can study the phenomenon — and it's true in much of science — without themselves changing. If you talk to the people who have been communicating with whales and orcas and dolphins and so on, they will all say right away that they've been deeply changed by the experience. I don't hear that from the people looking at UFO data. They think: oh, we'll analyze all this and then we'll establish some form. That's not going to happen.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Dr. Travis Taylor, whose scientific background and the work that he's doing in Utah with the ranch I highly respect, has said that he has some clearances in his own work, and he tried to see where other data could be found usefully from all the things we do in space now. So he looked at one particular project that's launching a special satellite for data acquisition in space. It's classified, but inside there are 15 different classified projects from different agencies. Remember, there isn't just one agency in the classified world, there are 14, and they all have their own task and their own business. And this is not that anybody is trying to hide anything, it's that the structure itself is impenetrable. So there has to be a change in our culture, there has to be a willingness to be open to not just physical data. So, to come back to your question, I think we're going to find that we need to go up a level. We need to change in order to be ready to communicate. As you know, in the book I've mentioned efforts in communication that have been ongoing for many years, and I think we need to change our attitude towards the whole problem.
